title: Circuit Hypernetworks for Quantum-Augmented Diffusion Language Models
authors: Xiaoqiang Wang, Mengyang Xiong, Jun Dai, Bang Liu
abstract: Language models can be adapted by changing the computations applied to individual tokens. Quantum circuits offer one such approach, but evaluating wider circuits inside a large model can be computationally demanding. Here we introduce HyperQ, which adds token-conditioned quantum residual branches to a frozen masked-diffusion language model. A quantum residual branch is a module in each transformer block that reads a token's hidden state, emits the coordinates of that token's circuit, executes it, and adds the measured values back through a residual connection. The backbone remains frozen, and only the added branches are trained. Within each branch, a lightweight circuit hypernetwork emits token-specific rotation angles, coupling strengths, and measurement axes in a shared sparse circuit structure. The required expectation values have an exact classical expression whose evaluation cost grows linearly with the qubit count, enabling circuits from 16 to 64 qubits to be trained within a 1.1-billion-parameter backbone. Across downstream benchmarks, increasing circuit width raises the average score from 47.65 to 54.30. At 64 qubits, HyperQ exceeds the backbone and its low-rank-adapted counterpart by 4.71 and 3.67 points, respectively. HyperQ is fine-tuned on 20,000 prompt-response pairs, compared with 200,000 for the classical baselines. These findings support token-conditioned circuit emission as a tractable architectural approach to quantum-augmented language modelling.
summary: This paper introduces HyperQ, a novel quantum-augmented architecture for diffusion language models. It solves the computational bottleneck of large quantum circuits by restricting the circuit structure to the IQP family, allowing for efficient, classical readout calculation. The resulting model significantly boosts language understanding performance across multiple benchmarks by incorporating token-specific quantum information processing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computational challenge of integrating quantum circuits into large language models while maintaining tractability as the circuit width increases.
main_result: The proposed HyperQ architecture successfully integrates quantum residual branches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks by scaling circuit width up to 64 qubits.
method: It uses a hypernetwork to emit token-conditioned parameters for a quantum residual branch, which is structured using the two-body instantaneous-quantum-polynomial (IQP) family.
model_or_system: The system is a frozen masked-diffusion language model backbone augmented by trainable quantum residual branches. The quantum computation is restricted to an IQP structure defined on a fixed sparse skeleton (ring + chord layers).
key_observables: Average benchmark scores (e.g., 54.30 at 64 qubits), and the expectation values $\langle Z_q angle$ measured for each qubit.
important_parameters: Circuit width (number of qubits, $n$), tested at 16, 32, and 64 qubits; the coupling strengths ($\omega_E$) are restricted to remain below $\pi/2$.
main_assumptions: The method relies on restricting the circuit to the IQP family to ensure the readout cost scales only linearly ($\Theta(n)$) with qubit count, and that the backbone remains frozen during training.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the HyperQ pipeline, showing the insertion of the quantum residual branch into the transformer block and the emission of circuit coordinates. One figure compares the constant readout cost ($\Theta(n)$) of the fixed skeleton versus the quadratic cost ($\Theta(n^2)$) of an all-to-all skeleton.
paper_structure: The paper introduces HyperQ, details the quantum residual branch structure using a hypernetwork, explains the mathematically tractable IQP readout mechanism, and validates the approach by showing performance gains across multiple downstream language model benchmarks.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, computationally efficient architectural blueprint for integrating quantum circuits into deep learning models, specifically by controlling the complexity of the quantum readout to remain polynomial in the number of qubits.
